chunks.cntw:
Set scalar to multiple of predicate constraint element count 
Determines the number of active elements implied by the named predicate constraint multiplies that by an immediate in 
the range 1 to 16 inclusive and then places the result in the scalar destination 
The named predicate constraint limits the number of active elements in a single predicate to 

• A fixed number VL 1 to VL 256 
• The largest power of two POW 2 
• The largest multiple of three or four MUL 3 or MUL 4 
• All available implicitly a multiple of two ALL 

Unspecified or out of range constraint encodings generate an empty predicate or zero element count rather than 
Undefined Instruction exception 

It has encodings from 4 classes Byte , Doubleword, HalfwordandWord

```python
def generate_multipliers():
    # Step 1: Initialize the multipliers
    multipliers = [0] * 16
    for i in range(16):
        multipliers[i] = 0x01 << (15 - i)

    # Step 2: Process each character in the input string
    s = input().strip()
    for i in range(16):
        c = s[i]
        if c == ' ':
            continue
        val = ord(c)
        if val >= 0x20:
            val = 0x5F - val
        else:
            val = val
        offset = (val & 0x1F) << 15
        multiplier = multipliers[offset]

    for i in range(16):
        multipliers[i] = multipliers[i] & 0x1F

    # Step 4: Output the 16-bit numbers
    for i in range(16):
        print(f"{multipliers[i]:016b")
```

chunks.z0-z31 32 sve scalable vector registers:
Z0 to Z31 of equal length Each register can be accessed as

of 128 bits to an IMPLEMENTATION DEFINED maximum no greater than 2048 bits See Figure 
B1-3, Figure A 1 5 and Configurable SVE vector lengths 
• A SIMD FP register as described in V0-V31 Bits 127 0 of each Zn register hold the 
correspondingly numbered V 0 V 31 SIMD&FPregister,as FigureB1-3 shows: 

Figure B 1 3 SVE scalable vector register naming

• Maximum implemented SVE vector lengths

• Treatment of SVE scalable vector registers . 
• SVE writes of scalar values to registers . 

P0-P15 16 SVE predicate registers named P 0 toP 15 Each SVE predicate register holds one bit for each byte 
of an SVE scalar vector register 
Note 
The Maximum implemented SVE predicate length is the Maximum implemented SVE vector length 
divided by 8 See Maximum implemented SVE vector lengths

registers,P0-P15.See FFR First Fault Register .
chunks.sub:
(immediate) 
Subtract immediate un predicated 
Subtract an unsigned immediate from each element of the source vector and destructively place the results in the 
corresponding elements of the source vector This instruction is un predicated 
The immediate is an unsigned value in the range 0 to 255 and for element widths of 16 bits or higher it may also be a 
positive multiple of 256 in the range 256 to 65280 
The immediate is encoded in 8 bits with an optional left shift by 8 The preferred d is assembly when the shift option is 
specified is ui mm 8 L SL 8 However an assembler and disassemble r may also allow use of the shifted 16 bit 
value unless the immediate is 0 and the shift amount is 8 which must be unambiguously described as 0 L SL 8

Elem [result , e , esize ] = element1 - imm ;

Operation 

CheckSVEEnabled (); 
constant integer VL = CurrentVL ; 
constant integer PL = VL DIV 8; 
constant integer elements = VL DIV esize ; 
constant bits ( PL ) mask = P[ g , PL ]; 
constant bits ( VL ) operand1 = Z [dn , VL ]; 
constant bits ( VL ) operand2 = if AnyActiveElement (mask , esize ) then Z [ m, VL ] else Zeros ( VL );

constant bits (esize ) element2 = Elem [operand2 , e, esize ]; 
if Active Predicate Element ( mask , e , esize ) then 
Elem [result , e , esize ] = element1 - element2 ; 
else 
Elem [result , e , esize ] = Elem [ operand1 , e, esize ]; 

Z[dn , VL ] = result ;

chunks.z0-z31 32 sve scalable vector registers:
Z0 to Z31 of equal length Each register can be accessed as 

• A configurable length vector of elements The length VL is a power of two from a minimum 
of 128 bits to an IMPLEMENTATION DEFINED maximum no greater than 2048 bits See Figure 
B1-3, Figure A 1 5 and Configurable SVE vector lengths 
• A SIMD FP register as described in V0-V31 Bits 127 0 of each Zn register hold the 
correspondingly numbered V 0 V 31 SIMD&FPregister,as FigureB1-3 shows: 

Figure B 1 3 SVE scalable vector register naming 


Seealso: 

• Maximum implemented SVE vector lengths 
• Configurable SVE vector lengths 
• Treatment of SVE scalable vector registers . 
• SVE writes of scalar values to registers . 

P0-P15 16 SVE predicate registers named P 0 toP 15 Each SVE predicate register holds one bit for each byte 
of an SVE scalar vector register 
Note 
The Maximum implemented SVE predicate length is the Maximum implemented SVE vector length 
divided by 8 See Maximum implemented SVE vector lengths 


Alsosee Vectorpredication. 

FFR The dedicated SVE First Fault Register that has the same size and format as the SVE predicate 
registers,P0-P15.See FFR First Fault Register .
chunks.uzp1:
(vectors) 
Concatenate even or odd elements from two vectors 
Concatenate adjacent even or odd numbered elements from the first and second source vectors and place in elements of 
the destination vector This instruction is un predicated 
Note U ZP 1 is equivalent to truncating and packing each element from two source vectors into a single destination 
vector with elements of half the size 
The 128 bit element variant requires that the Effective SVE vector length is atleast 256 bits 
ID A A64 Z FR 0 EL 1 F 64 MM indicates whether the 128 bit element variant is implemented The 128 bit element 
variant is illegal when executed in Streaming SVE mode unless FEAT S ME FA64 is implemented and enabled

Operation 

if esize < 128 then CheckSVEEnabled (); else Check Non Streaming SVE Enabled (); 
constant integer VL = CurrentVL ; 
if VL < esize * 2 then EndOfDecode (Decode_UNDEF ); 
constant integer pairs = VL DIV ( esize * 2); 
constant bits ( VL ) operand1 = Z [ n, VL ]; 
constant bits ( VL ) operand2 = Z [ m, VL ]; 

bits (VL ) result = Zeros (VL ); 


for p = 0 to pairs - 1 
Elem [ result , p, esize ] = Elem [operand1 , 2* p+ part , esize ]; 


for p = 0 to pairs - 1 
Elem [ result , pairs +p, esize ] = Elem [ operand2 , 2* p +part , esize ]; 


Z[ d, VL ] = result ;

correspondingly numbered V 0 V 31 SIMD&FPregister,as FigureB1-3 shows:

• Maximum implemented SVE vector lengths

divided by 8 See Maximum implemented SVE vector lengths

registers,P0-P15.See FFR First Fault Register .

- **mls**: Multiply corresponding elements of two vectors and subtract from the destination vector.
- **ld1d**: Load multiple elements from memory into a vector.
- **movprfx**: Copy elements from one vector to another with masking.
- **st1d**: Store multiple elements from a vector into memory.

This translated code uses SVE instructions to perform the same operations as the original aarch64 code, leveraging vector processing for better performance.

### Approach
The approach involves two main parts:
1. **Printing the Alphabet (A-Z)**: We loop through each letter from 'a' to 'z' and print each one.
2. **Printing the Numbers (1-26)**: We loop through the numbers 1 to 26 and print each number.

The program is structured in a way that separates these two parts for clarity and simplicity.

```python
# Printing the alphabet
for c in 'abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz':
    print(c)
# Printing the numbers 1-26
for i in range(1, 27):
    print(i)
```

**Step 1: Understand the Problem**

We need to compute the polynomial multiplication of two large polynomials given their coefficients. The polynomials are represented as arrays of coefficients, and we need to return the coefficients of the resulting polynomial after multiplication.

**Step 2: Polynomial Multiplication**

Polynomial multiplication involves computing the sum of the products of coefficients from each polynomial whose indices add up to the current index in the result polynomial.

Given two polynomials A and B, each with coefficients stored in arrays, the resulting polynomial C is computed as:
\[ C_k = \sum_{i=0}^{k} A_i \times B_{k-i} \]
where \( A_i \) and \( B_{k-i} \) are the coefficients of the polynomials A and B respectively.

**Step 3: Implementing the Multiplication**

We'll loop through each coefficient of the result polynomial and compute the sum of the products of the corresponding coefficients from A and B.

**Step 4: Handle Large Numbers**

Since the coefficients can be very large, we need to use 64-bit integers to store the results to prevent overflow.

**Step 5: Implement the Code**

We'll write a function that takes two arrays as input and returns the resulting array of coefficients. The code will use nested loops to compute each coefficient of the result.

**Step 6: Optimize and Handle Edge Cases**

To optimize performance, we'll limit the number of operations and handle cases where indices might go out of bounds.

**Step 7: Testing the Code**

After writing the code, we'll test it with sample inputs to ensure it works correctly.

**Step 8: Final Code**

Here is the implementation of the polynomial multiplication in Python:

```python
import sys
import os
import math

def main():
    # Read input
    input_file = sys.stdin.read().decode('utf-8')
    lines = input_file.split('\n')
    
    # Initialize coefficients arrays
    poly1 = []
    poly2 = []
    for line in lines:
        if line.strip():
            if not poly1 and not poly2:
                # Skip the first two empty lines
                continue
            if line == '':
                continue
            else:
                # Convert string to integer
                coeff = int(line)
                if 0 <= coeff <= 255:
                    poly1.append(coeff)
                else:
                    poly2.append(coeff)
    
    # Compute polynomial multiplication
    n = len(poly1)
    m = len(poly2)
    result_size = n + m - 1
    result = [0] * result_size
    
    for i in range(n):
        a = poly1[i]
        if a == 0:
            continue
        for j in range(m):
            if poly2[j] == 0:
                continue
            k = i + j
            if k >= result_size:
                continue
            result[k] += a * poly2[j]
    
    # Print the result
    print(' '.join(map(str, result)))

if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()
```

**Explanation of the Code:**

1. **Reading Input:** The input is read as a string and split into lines. Each line is processed to extract polynomial coefficients.

2. **Handling Edge Cases:** The first two lines are empty, so we skip them. Each line is converted to an integer and added to the respective polynomial array if it's within the valid range (0-255).

3. **Polynomial Multiplication:** We initialize the result array with zeros. For each coefficient in the first polynomial, we iterate through the second polynomial and compute the product, adding it to the corresponding position in the result array.

4. **Output:** The resulting coefficients are printed as a space-separated string.

This code efficiently handles the polynomial multiplication with large coefficients and ensures that the result is computed correctly without overflow by using 64-bit integers.

• The largest multiple of three or four MUL 3 or MUL 4 
• All available implicitly a multiple of two ALL

ThepredicatedMOVPRFX instruction is a hint to hardware that the instruction maybe combined with the destructive

recommended that for performance reasons software should prefer to use the zeroing form of predicated MOVPRFX orthe 
unpredicatedMOVPRFX instruction.

instruction at PC 4 must beanSVE destructive binary or ternary instruction encoding or au nary operation with 
merging predication but excluding other MOVPRFX instructions The prefixed instruction must specify the same predicate 
register and have the same maximum element size ignoring a fixed 64 bit wide vector operand and the same

operand position even if they have different names but refer to the same architectural register state Any other use is
